# The Two Types of Programmer

Developing a software product that's essential to the survival of a business breeds different behaviours to developing software in other businesses.

e.g. Compare working at Google to developing software in a bank.

Developers don't split themselves into pools of these 2 behaviours. So dealing with the second type of behaviour is a challenge for software product companies (as is dealing with the first type of behaviour for non-software-product companies). What behaviours have non-software-product developers learned?

Martin Fowler writes influentially for the non-software-product developer audience. His [writings](https://martinfowler.com/articles/creating-integrated-tech-strategy.html#quality) give us some insights into their practices. The main characteristics are:

* General rules rather than specific cases. This is the opposite of small product companies which start by building something (the specific) then grow (the general).  
* Many words.  
* Written for decision makers, not for builders. This is the opposite of small product companies where the founders and early employees are builders.

These qualities imply a top-down, talk-heavy, general approach to software development. 

**How can we use the above observations to help non-software-product developers orient themselves in a software product company?**

* What skills and work habits learned in the non-product world can these developers put to immediate use in a product company?  
* What are the fastest adjustments they can make to become more effective in product work?


There's a well-known answer to these questions. It's what you always should do when starting work in a new job, unless you are a transformational manager, consultant or in a similar job where your major incentive is to change existing practices: *Primum non nocere, don't fix it if it's not broken, …*

This raises the question of why we allowed (and in many cases encouraged) changes from effective to less effective practices in the past. Once again, the answer seems obvious. We were focussed on the few things we did wrong rather than the many things we did right. Slightly less obviously, we were allowed to do so because of the success of MF and the people supporting it. Our early success allowed us to operate at lower productivity levels without dire consequences.

**How does thinking about the above history help us today, if it does at all?**

We need to think in terms of the business success/failure that our current development work will create in the future. Not in terms of the current  business success our previous development created. (The well-worn analogy is that we need to start driving down the freeway by looking ahead, not in our rear-view mirrors.) Think carefully about incentives, metrics and what "accountability" means

It would be nice for developers to have simple discussions about what we are building. Framing discussions in terms of today's business problems distracts from this. The stuff that sales people and executives care and talk about is important to them and to our business. But the most valuable thing developers can do is build products that will make our business successful in the future.

The successful startup PaperCut's business was based on building stuff that people needed. I expect non-software-product developers could enjoy this as much as we did, if we just *did* it, rather than try to *talk* our way of the state we got ourselves into.

**This seems simple. Why are we finding it difficult?**  
Developers who think of themselves as Fowler-bots may have a mental model of software development that includes the top-down, wordy world of enterprise development. Maybe they wait for PMs to tell them to do things, rather than doing them.

Enterprise-world (and its symbiotic partner consultant-world) gives a lot of power to leaders and talkers, in contrast to startup-world where the heroes are people who get stuff done, either by doing it themselves or helping other people do it.  
Something we don't talk about is that coding is usually a small part of developer work (and getting smaller with AI). In *startup-world*, I think about problems then type solutions into my computer. In *enterprise-world*, I expect most developer work is in understanding business requirements (except for where developer work gets outsourced to low wage countries). These ways of working are not that different. A substantial fraction of our current inefficiency comes from splitting that problem analysis into separate groups. In a similar way we have split testing and tech support into separate groups. (Consultants are cunning enough to warn of the problems of siloing roles while doing this. Splitting then recombining roles provides an endless cycle of work for them.)  We old-timers can remember how much fun it was to combine all these roles. It will probably be just as much fun for any practical minded developer from any background.

# What makes growth hard?

PaperCut is like most startups that have grown into medium size companies.  
Startup-world is different to enterprise-world. The culture changes going from one to the other are tortuous. Startups are one of the few ways of enjoying the benefits of industrialisation (huge improvements in efficiency due to specialisation) without suffering from the [alienation](https://uregina.ca/~gingrich/250j2703.htm) it usually brings.

*... he does not fulfil himself in his work but denies himself, has a feeling of misery rather than well-being, does not develop freely his mental and physical energies but is physically exhausted and mentally debased.  The worker, therefore, feels himself at home only during his leisure time, whereas at work he feels homeless.  His work is not voluntary but imposed, forced labour.  It is not the satisfaction of a need, but only a means for satisfying other needs.*

* In startups there is a joy in building a product with a few co-workers and seeing customers use it. Startup employees enjoy the benefits of industrialisation without suffering the alienation  
* In enterprise-world, workers need to get their joy in other ways. e.g meetings or using new software frameworks.


These are our underlying motivations built up over years of working. Training courses are unlikely to change them.  
Melbourne has many more enterprise jobs than startup jobs and people don't stay in jobs forever. Being a pure startup person would be a major career risk.

**Why not embrace *enterprise-world*?**

Startups are the outlier in the modern world. Enterprises enjoy the benefits of scale. Scale gives the improvements in efficiency due to specialisation and other benefits.  
Startups need to achieve efficiency in other ways, such as by producing much more functionality per employee as PaperCut did in the early 2010s.  
But we  haven't needed that efficiency for some time. Why not give up on it?  
We were allowed to do so because of the success of MF and the people supporting it. Our early success allowed us to operate at lower productivity levels without dire consequences.  
Our market has changed and we need new products. Enterprise-level productivity is not going to be sufficient until we build those products.  
Then we can move back to our current productivity levels until the market changes again.  
And so on. A cycle of building then sliding back into inefficiency?

**Why not stay hungry all the time?**

It's hard to stay hungry when you are surrounded by all the food you just grew.  
That's true of most people most of the time. But we all know of many exceptions.  
Some people are driven to be active all the time. Some people are always curious. Even when they don't need to be in times of plenty.  
These people are the ones who are ready for changes in the environment. Why not encourage this behaviour?  
This is not a new idea. Companies have had R\&D departments for years. (edited) 

# Silicon Valley

We can learn from thinking critically about Silicon Valley [fiction](https://www.thepsmiths.com/p/review-scaling-people-by-claire-hughes).  
There’s another, very different reason managers need to be experts in whatever it is their team is doing, and it has to do with morale. A subordinate in any sort of hierarchical organisation needs to see that his superior can do his own job as well or better than he can. Almost everybody gets this. In a high-pressure commercial kitchen, if a chef or sous-chef doesn’t like the performance of one of their line cooks, they will often leap in, take over that cook’s station, and begin “expediting.” This has a dual purpose: it both relieves a genuine production bottleneck, and also acts as a showy demonstration of prowess, reminding everybody that they got to be the boss through excellence. At the better tech companies, those managing software engineers are always former engineers themselves, and often the very best of the lot. Just like a chef would do, an engineering manager needs to be able to seize a computer and begin expediting under pressure, both to solve a real problem and as a dominance display. But it’s not just about keeping the troops in line, it’s about inspiring them. Nothing motivates a soldier like seeing his commander leading the charge, weapon in hand

# Wealth of Nations

Agricultural work is a more desirable situation than industrial work because the owner is in complete control. Adam [Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wealth_of_Nations#Agricultural_jobs) said:

*In our North American colonies, where uncultivated land is still to be had upon easy terms, no manufactures for distant sale have ever yet been established in any of their towns. When an artificer has acquired a little more stock than is necessary for carrying on his own business in supplying the neighbouring country, he does not, in North America, attempt to establish with it a manufacture for more distant sale, but employs it in the purchase and improvement of uncultivated land. From artificer he becomes planter, and neither the large wages nor the easy subsistence which that country affords to artificers, can bribe him rather to work for other people than for himself. **He feels that an artificer is the servant of his customers, from whom he derives his subsistence; but that a planter who cultivates his own land, and derives his necessary subsistence from the labour of his own family, is really a master, and independent of all the world.***
